abstract.title: Significance
abstract.p: Blood clotting is a balanced process that ensures rapid control of bleeding without causing thrombosis. Factor IXa, a protease in the blood coagulation pathway, exemplifies this requirement for balance. Its deficiency causes the bleeding defect in hemophilia B and a gain in its function is linked to a higher risk of thrombosis. We show that an RNA aptamer developed to specifically inhibit IXa binds to a remote exosite in the protease domain and allosterically distorts the active site. Plasticity in the catalytic site of IXa associated with exosite binding suggests a unique mechanism for the regulation of IXa function and establishes the exosite as a molecular target for drug development.

Hemostasis relies on a reaction network of serine proteases and their cofactors to form a blood clot. Coagulation factor IXa (protease) plays an essential role in hemostasis as evident from the bleeding disease associated with its absence. RNA aptamers specifically targeting individual coagulation factors have potential as anticoagulants and as probes of the relationship between structure and function. Here, we report X-ray structures of human factor IXa without a ligand bound to the active site either in the apo-form or in complex with an inhibitory aptamer specific for factor IXa. The aptamer binds to an exosite in the catalytic domain and allosterically distorts the active site. Our studies reveal a conformational ensemble of IXa states, wherein large movements of Trp215 near the active site drive functional transitions between the closed (aptamer-bound), latent (apo), and open (substrate-bound) states. The latent state of the apo-enzyme may bear on the uniquely poor catalytic activity of IXa compared to other coagulation proteases. The exosite, to which the aptamer binds, has been implicated in binding VIIIa and heparin, both of which regulate IXa function. Our findings reveal the importance of exosite-driven allosteric modulation of IXa function and new strategies to rebalance hemostasis for therapeutic gain.

body.p: Mammalian blood forms a clot at the site of vascular damage in the hemostatic response to trauma. This balanced process must be simultaneously prompt to stanch blood loss and limited in space to prevent propagation across the vasculature to cause thrombosis (1). Blood clotting results from a highly regulated proteolytic network, in which inactive precursors (zymogens) circulating in blood plasma are converted into active coagulation factors (2, 3). Activated coagulation proteases typically form an enzymic complex with a membrane-bound cofactor to greatly enhance catalytic activity toward their macromolecular substrates (4, 5). These features are exemplified by the intrinsic Xase complex of a protease, IXa; cofactor, VIIIa; and substrate, X. The essential role of the intrinsic Xase is evident from the equivalent bleeding phenotypes associated with either the deficiency of factor VIII (hemophilia A) or IX (hemophilia B) (6).

Alone, factor IXa is an exceptionally poor enzyme in comparison to the other coagulation proteases despite their high sequence homology, a common chymotrypsin-like fold of the catalytic domain, and identical geometry of the catalytic triad of Asp102, His57, and Ser195 (numbered according to the homologous residues in chymotrypsinogen) (7). Factor IXa interacts with membranes and membrane-bound factor VIIIa to achieve a 105-fold increase in catalytic activity for the activation of factor X (8). The understanding of how cofactors work to enhance cleavage of the cognate biological substrate remains incomplete in many physiological systems, such as blood coagulation, fibrinolysis, kinin–kallikrein system, complement, extracellular matrix remodeling, apoptosis, embryonic polarity, etc. (9).

A crucial role in cofactor binding by coagulation factors VIIa, IXa, and Xa has been assigned to an exosite region in the catalytic domain flanked by 126-, 162-, and 230-helices (10–12), also structurally related to exosite 2 of thrombin (13). Interestingly, residue Arg170 in the catalytic domain of factor IXa (the position 338FL in the full-length protein) is a part of that exosite and is associated with unexpected bidirectional effects on hemostasis. The missense mutation Arg170Pro undermines IXa activity and causes an inherited bleeding disorder (14, 15), while the naturally occurring gain-of-function mutations Arg170Leu in factor IX Padua and Arg170Gln in factor IX Shanghai lead to a several-fold higher risk of venous thromboembolism (16–18) (https://www.factorix.org/). Recently, the use of the Padua gain-of-function mutant has resulted in a major advance in the treatment of hemophilia B by gene therapy (19).

RNA aptamers selected against individual coagulation factors are promising therapeutic agents and have proved invaluable as molecular tools to delineate the role of specific binding events in hemostasis and thrombosis. We have previously developed an inhibitory RNA aptamer (DTRI-177) derived from 9.3t that specifically binds IXa (20, 21). Although the mechanism of inhibition by DTRI-177 was previously unclear, it proved an efficient anticoagulant in the highly thrombotic preclinical model of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) (22). Here, we use DTRI-177 as a high-affinity probe to shed light on structural correlates of factor IXa function. We describe new X-ray structures in apo- and aptamer-bound forms vs. the known substrate-bound form and discover structural transitions associated with substrate binding. The aptamer binds to the exosite and allosterically inhibits the active site via flexible 170- and 220-loops and Trp215 residue connecting it to the substrate-binding pockets. This study provides the first direct evidence for exosite-mediated allosteric control of factor IXa and highlights the molecular features utilized by aptamers for the specific recognition of coagulation proteases. These findings illustrate the role of allostery in IXa function and suggest the exosite as a target for allosteric modulators with potential for therapeutic gain.

sec.title: DTRI-177 Is Bound to an Exosite in the Catalytic Domain of Human Factor IXa.
sec.p: Two recombinant variants of human factor IX, amenable to crystallization, were expressed by truncating the N-terminal domains, mutating the catalytic Ser195 to Ala (chymotrypsinogen numbering) and replacing Arg at the proteolytic activation sites with the furin-recognition sequence (Arg–Arg–Lys–Arg) (Fig. 1A). Coexpression of the factor IX constructs with secreted and soluble furin in AV12 cells resulted in the production of the truncated IXa variants that were then purified from conditioned medium and used for crystallography. The location of the molecular surface on IXa targeted by DTRI-177 was determined from the crystal structure of the aptamer–protease complex obtained at 2.6 Å resolution by X-ray diffraction on crystals of DTRI-177 with ΔGlaΔEGF1-hIXaS195A (PDB ID: 8EPK) (structure “i”), (Fig. 1B). We also solved structures of apo-factor IXa from X-ray diffraction experiments on crystals of apo-ΔGla-hIXaS195A at 1.9 Å resolution (PDB ID: 8EPH) (structure “ii”) and apo-ΔGlaΔEGF1-hIXaS195A at 2.5 Å resolution (PDB ID: 8EPC) (SI Appendix, Table S1). Henceforth, the “apo-form” refers to 8EPH (structure “ii”), which is the most complete structure of human factor IXa published thus far and the first structure of IXa without a ligand at the active site (Fig. 1C and SI Appendix, Fig. S1). Measurements of the binding of biotinylated DTRI-177 to all factor IXa variants revealed that the designed truncations or mutations did not appreciably affect aptamer binding affinity (SI Appendix, Fig. S2 and Table S2).

sec.p: In the cocrystal structure (i) of the aptamer–protease complex (8EPK), DTRI-177 does not occlude the active site of factor IXa and is bound to a remote exosite on the catalytic domain (Fig. 1B) analogous to the anion-binding exosite-2 of thrombin (23). The interaction interface on the surface of factor IXa involves an extended area of 1,100 Å2 covering three α-helices and a deep groove. Pockets inside the groove are primarily contacted by the aptamer ribonucleotides U9 and U19 (Movie S1). Nucleobases, 2′-modified ribose rings, and the phosphodiester backbone form contacts with factor IXa residues, some of which, Arg165, Asn178, and Arg233, have previously been implicated in interactions with heparin (11) and factor VIIIa (24). Binding of DTRI-177 to the exosite has a distant effect on the active site and stabilizes a conformation in which the S1 substrate-binding pocket is blocked (Figs. 1B and 2). Distortion of the active site arising from DTRI-177 binding explains inhibition of IXa by the aptamer.

A close-up view of the active site region (red) is shown for these states in the second row. (B) Comparison of active site geometry for apo- vs. antithrombin-bound structures of factor IXa (8EPH, 3KCG), factor Xa (1C5M, 2GD4), and thrombin (3U69, 1SR5) illustrating the closed state of the S1 pocket in apo-factor IXa not seen in apo-factor Xa or apo-thrombin. The closed form of the active site in DTRI-177 -bound IXa is not evident for factor Xa containing an aptamer bound to the analogous exosite. Catalytic triad is shown in red, Tyr99 (IXa and Xa) and Leu99 (thrombin) in grey, and Trp215 in yellow. Second-order rate constants for the inhibition by antithrombin without heparin are shown in the Right margin (25). (C) Superimposed structures of factor IXa in three functional states (i), (ii), and (iii). Location of the S1 pocket, 170-loop, 215-219 region, 220-225 region (220-loop), and movements of the Trp215 side chain (Å) are highlighted. (D) Measurements of initial rate of fluorogenic substrate cleavage (300 µM) by factor IXa (150 nM) with increasing concentrations of DTRI-177.

sec.title: Conformational Ensemble of Factor IXa Determines Active Site Function.
sec.p: High-resolution structures of factor IXa, representing different functional states of the catalytic domain, provide additional insights into function (Fig. 2A). Comparisons of the apo-form (ii) with the previously published Michaelis complex of IXa bound to antithrombin (PDB ID: 3KCG; structure “iii”) (26), unexpectedly revealed an already suboptimal and latent conformation of the S1 pocket in apo-factor IXa (Figs. 1C and 2 B, Top Center). While the Michaelis complex of IXaS195A with antithrombin illustrates a typical substrate-bound conformation where the Arg side-chain of the substrate-like inhibitor is inserted into an open S1 pocket of the active site (Fig. 2 B, Top Right), the apo-form of IXaS195A cannot accommodate a substrate, unless Trp215 is displaced by 4.7 Å and the 215 to 225 backbone is reorganized to open the S1 pocket (Fig. 2C and Movie S2). Experimental structures deposited in PDB reveal that, in contrast to IXa, both apo- and substrate-bound forms of factor Xa (Fig. 2 B, Center row) or thrombin (Fig. 2 B, Bottom row) exhibit an open S1 pocket. Together, these points imply that IXa may be unique, wherein the apo form of the protease contains an immature active site that needs further optimization for catalytic function. The collapsed active site geometry may have bearing on why IXa is an order of magnitude less reactive toward antithrombin than factor Xa and thrombin (Fig. 2 B, Right column).

The apo-form of factor IXa (ii) occupies an intermediate position between the aptamer-bound (i) and substrate-bound (iii) forms (Fig. 2C). This position is characterized by substantial displacements in the 215 to 225 backbone defined by good electron density and by high flexibility of Phe174, Tyr177, and Trp215 residues as indicated by faint electron density for these side chains (SI Appendix, Fig. S3B). The second structure of apo-ΔGlaΔEGF1-hIXaS195A (8EPC) additionally shows poorer electron density in the 215 to 225 polypeptide backbone raising the possibility of flexibility in the 215 to 225 polypeptide as well as the sidechains noted (not graphically illustrated). For factor IXa, Tyr99 and Trp215 occupy distinct configurations in the aptamer-bound (i) and apo- (ii) forms with a 6.8 Å translocation of Trp215 side chain toward catalytic His57 upon aptamer binding (Fig. 2C), accompanied by a complete closure of S1 pocket (Movie S3). While the 215 to 219 region clearly differs between all three forms, both the binding of DTRI-177 to the exosite and the binding of substrate to the active site yielded similar conformations for the 220 to 225 backbone and the 170- loop of factor IXa (Fig. 2C and SI Appendix, Fig. S3), giving rise to the question of how allosteric communication between the exosite and active site occurs. In contrast to IXa, equivalent active site geometries are observed for factor Xa bound to the RNA aptamer 11F7t (27), the apo form, and Xa bound to antithrombin (Fig. 2 B, Center row). Although 11F7t binds to an analogous exosite in the protease domain of Xa, lack of effects on accessibility of the S1 pocket correlate with the inability of 11F7t to inhibit peptidyl substrate cleavage by Xa (28). These underlie the unique features of factor IXa wherein regulation can be related to the latent conformation of its apo-form and may be realized through structural rearrangements of the flexible active site region.

sec.title: Allosteric Inhibitory Effect on the Catalytic Activity.
sec.p: Our finding that DTRI-177 binds to a region of IXa distinct from the active site questions whether the associated collapse of the S1 binding pocket is sufficient to explain the previously established ability of the aptamer to inhibit the catalytic function of IXa (21). We extended prior studies to assess the effects of DTRI-177 on the reaction between catalytically active IXa and the suicide substrate, antithrombin, in the presence of the heparin pentasaccharide. The covalent complex of factor IXa and antithrombin was resolved on SDS-PAGE gel and could be followed as the reaction proceeded (SI Appendix, Fig. S4A). Preincubation with a saturating concentration of DTRI-177 prevented the formation of the serpin–IXa complex (SI Appendix, Fig. S4A). Quantitative densitometry analysis indicated an approximate 100-fold reduction in the rate of reaction with antithrombin (SI Appendix, Fig. S4B). The superposed structures of factor IXa in the complex with aptamer (8EPK) and IXa in complex with antithrombin bound to pentasaccharide (3KCG) (26) illustrate that the aptamer and serpin bind to opposing faces of the protease without steric clash (SI Appendix, Fig. S4C), further highlighting the allosteric action of DTRI-177.

Inhibition of catalytic function of IXa by DTRI-177 was confirmed by initial velocity studies of the cleavage of a fluorescent peptidyl substrate. The aptamer caused near stoichiometric inhibition of substrate cleavage, further pointing to the importance of the allosteric effect of DTRI-177 on the active site of factor IXa in impairing protease function (Fig. 2D). Addition of the peptidyl substrate following preincubation of IXa with DTRI-177 yielded progress curves with a pronounced and extended lag (SI Appendix, Fig. S5). This suggests that any DTRI-177-dependent perturbation of the active site that leads to inhibition can slowly be reversed by the substrate in a concentration-dependent manner. These functional measurements are in-line with the structural changes observed in active site geometry comparing the aptamer-bound form (i) to the substrate-bound form (iii) (Fig. 2C) implicating exosite-mediated allosteric regulation of factor IXa function by the aptamer.

sec.title: Bases of Specific Recognition of the Exosite.
sec.p: DTRI-177 binds factor IXa with a subnanomolar affinity and high selectivity over other coagulation factors (SI Appendix, Table S3). In complex with IXa, DTRI-177 is in a double helical hairpin-like conformation along most of its length with the exception of ribonucleotides U9 and U19, which twist outward from one face of the helix to interact with the protease (Fig. 3A). The shape of DTRI-177 is complementary to the surface of the exosite on factor IXa and positions the nucleobase of U9 to fit into a pocket surrounded by positively charged residues of the 126- and 162-helices and by a part of the 170-loop. U9 belongs to the conserved A8U9A10-motif wherein substitution of A’s with G’s was shown to lead to a loss of factor IXa binding (20). The resolved cocrystal structure (PDB ID: 8EPK) provides a rational explanation for the high affinity of IXa binding and the role played by A8U9A10-motif. Nucleobases A8 and A10, both located near the aptamer Mg2+-binding site, form a π–π stacking interaction that produces a kink in the backbone that allows U9 to unwind toward the factor IXa pocket and interact with Asn129A; Lys132; Leu162; and Val163 (Fig. 3A and Movie S1).

(A) The scheme of DTRI-177 showing its secondary structure and snapshots of the interactions formed with factor IXa. In the scheme, direct contacts to factor IXa are denoted; ribonucleotides C11, C12, U16 that did not form interactions and were missing in the electron density are fogged. In the snapshots taken from Movie S1, ribonucleotides A8 and A10 defining the binding to factor IXa are shown. The 2mFo-DFc electron density map is contoured at 1.5 σ (blue mesh) around the selected residues. (B–D) Structures of the aptamer–protease complexes for DTRI-177 (cyan)—factor IXa (PDB ID: 8EPK) (B), 11F7t (light red)—factor Xa (PDB ID: 5VOE) (C), and Toggle-25t (green)—thrombin (PDB ID: 3DD2) (D) are shown in the standard orientation. Na+ ion violet. Corresponding magnified views of the exosite surface are shown with the interacting protein surfaces rendered in blue. (E) Complex formed between heparin and anion binding exosite-2 of thrombin resolved in the structure of the thrombin–antithrombin–heparin complex (PDB ID: 1TB6) also shown in the standard orientation. (F) Sequence alignment of part of the factor IXa catalytic domain encompassing the DTRI-177 interacting surface from the indicated species. (G) DTRI-177-induced prolongation of the activated partial thromboplastin clotting time in plasma from humans, cynomolgus monkeys, cows, pigs, Beagle dogs, rabbits, Sprague-Dawley rats, and C57/Bl6 mice.

sec.p: To probe the basis of specificity for DTRI-177, we compared our structure of the complex with previously solved structures of factor Xa and thrombin bound to their specific RNA aptamers 11F7t and Toggle-25t, respectively. The anti-Xa and anti-thrombin aptamers target structurally related exosites on their cognate proteases (Fig. 3 B–D, Top). The landscape of the interacting surfaces reveals individualized exosite geometries for each coagulation protease, despite high conservation of the exosite residues, such as Arg93, Lys/Arg126, Arg165, Arg233, and Lys/Arg240 (Fig. 3 B–D, Bottom). Unwound ribonucleotides, U9 and U19 of DTRI-177, C6 and A15 of Toggle-25t, and A10 and A21 of 11F7t, are differentially positioned within the exosite groove and surrounded by positively charged side chains. In contrast to the selective binding of specific RNA aptamers, heparin binds to a wide range of proteins in the cardiovascular system, including coagulation proteases (SI Appendix, Table S3). The heparin-binding exosite on the surface of thrombin (PDB ID: 1TB6) overlaps the site specifically targeted by Toggle-25t (Fig. 3 D and E). However, heparin polar groups contact the exosite surface superficially and do not interact with residues inside the groove, thus making only charge-dependent interactions, which explains its reduced selectivity. These points illustrate how high specificity for aptamer binding derives from individual features of the RNA sequence that are translated into its shape complementary to the exosite geometry of the target protease.

Additionally, the exosite residues contribute to the species specificity of the aptamer to human factor IXa. Aptamer-interacting residues are highly conserved in all known mammalian sequences of factor IX (representing 101 animal species). Surprisingly, Lys132, Leu162, and Arg233, which contact DTRI-177, are replaced by Asn, Phe and Trp, respectively, in rabbit factor IX (Fig. 3F). To test the implied importance of these residues, the ability of DTRI-177 to inhibit blood clotting was examined in plasma from humans, rabbits and other laboratory animal species using the activated partial thromboplastin time. Clotting time was prolonged by increasing concentrations of DTRI-177 up to threefold for human, monkey, cow, dog, rat, and mouse plasma (Fig. 3G). Clotting times in pig plasma were more prominently prolonged by DTRI-177 primarily because of a lower baseline clotting time. In contrast, clotting times in rabbit plasma were unchanged even at 4 µM aptamer, implying a defective interaction of DTRI-177 with rabbit factor IX and IXa. Mixing experiments were performed using human hemophilia B plasma reconstituted with 10% (v/v) human or rabbit plasma. Increasing concentrations of DTRI-177 again failed to prolong clotting in human factor IX deficient plasma reconstituted with 10% rabbit plasma (SI Appendix, Fig. S6). These studies rule out potentially trivial explanations for the apparent inability of DTRI-177 to prolong clotting in rabbit plasma.

sec.title: Exosite Configuration and Competition between Ligands.
sec.p: All three structures (i), (ii), and (iii) exhibit equivalent exosite configurations (Fig. 4 A–C). Using binding studies, we further assessed whether there was functional evidence for exosite plasticity to complement rearrangements in the active site of factor IXa. In one set of experiments, three forms of IX/IXa were titrated against Alexa Fluor 594 conjugated DTRI-177 and the binding of aptamer was inferred from increases in fluorescence anisotropy. Zymogen factor IX and apo-IXaS195A yielded equivalent equilibrium dissociation constants, while factor IXa covalently inactivated with Phe–Phe–Arg–chloromethyl ketone (hFIXa-FFR) showed only a modest (threefold) decrease in affinity for the aptamer (Fig. 4 D–F and SI Appendix, Table S2). These findings were independently confirmed in a second set of experiments utilizing biolayer interferometry (BLI) (SI Appendix, Fig. S2 and Table S2). Although allosteric effects at the active site associated with exosite binding are obvious, reciprocal linkage between active site ligation on exosite binding is less clear, implying that the full thermodynamic cycle has not been accounted for. Together, the data are consistent with a stable exosite configuration, which remains unchanged upon aptamer or substrate binding. Such stability, derived from rigidity of the α-helices in the exosite, also results in similar affinities of heparin to factor IX and IXa.

caption.p: Probing the conformation of the IXa exosite with DTRI-177. (A–C) Comparison of exosite geometry in factor IXa in the states i (A), ii (B), and iii (C) illustrating the absence of significant differences between the states. Exosite residues interacting with DTRI-177 are shown in blue. (D–F) Fluorescence anisotropy of Alexa Fluor 594-labeled DTRI-177 (30 nM—red; 50 nM—black) measured with increasing concentrations of factor IX (D), factor IXaS195A with free active site (E), factor IXa with the stabilized active site, hFIXa-FFR (F). Upon binding of factors IX and IXa, the fluorescence intensity was decreased by at most 3% (Fmax/F0 = 1.03). Lines were obtained by nonlinear regression analysis as described in ref. 5 and SI Appendix, Extended Materials and Methods, which yielded the following parameters: the initial value of anisotropy for the aptamer alone, r0, 0.1532 ± 0.0007; the maximal increase in anisotropy, Δrmax, 0.0545 ± 0.0038. The values of KD and stoichiometry are shown in SI Appendix, Table S2.

sec.p: If two ligands bind to overlapping molecular surfaces in the same molecule, then binding of one ligand is expected to interfere with binding of the second. Hence, DTRI-177 and heparin, both targeting overlapping surfaces in the exosite of IXa, may compete with each other for binding. In the first approach, we examined the ability of heparin to affect binding of IXa to immobilized DTRI-177 by BLI (Fig. 5A). The equilibrium binding curves obtained at increasing concentrations of heparin indicate a dose-dependent increase in the effective KD for the interaction of IXa with immobilized DTRI-177. In the second approach, the ability of DTRI-177 to affect the retention of IX and IXa on a heparin affinity matrix was examined (Fig. 5B). When preincubated with a saturating concentration of DTRI-177, factors IX and IXa lost the ability to be retained by the heparin affinity matrix and eluted mainly in the flow-through fraction (Fig. 5 B, Right). These experiments indicate steric competition between these ligands of the IXa exosite despite different binding mechanisms at play.

caption.p: DTRI-177 and heparin bind to the exosite in factor IX and IXa in a mutually exclusive manner. (A) Binding kinetics of factor IXa to biotinylated DTRI-177 measured by biolayer interferometry either in the absence or presence of 5, 10, and 50 µM low molecular weight heparin (3 kDa). Fitting with equilibrium competition model resulted in IXa-binding affinity (KD) of 0.35 ± 0.04 nM for DTRI-177 and 2.5 ± 0.3 µM for low molecular weight heparin. (B) Affinity chromatography of factor IX alone (Left) or factor IX preincubated with DTRI-177 (Right) on heparin Sepharose and elution with a gradient of increasing NaCl.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Factor IXa is an enigmatic serine protease. While homologous coagulation proteases exhibit substantial reactivity (kcat to peptidyl substrates up to 10 to 100 s−1), factor IXa is much worse both in cleaving peptidyl substrates (kcat up to 0.1 s−1) and in its inhibition by antithrombin (Fig. 2 B, Right column). Previously, the low activity of IXa was explained by a “gatekeeper” role of Lys98 and Tyr99 proposed to prevent access to the active site (29). Together with later claims about substrate- and cofactor-assisted maturation of the active site, those studies were based on limited evidence that involved structures of IXa captured with substrate analogs in the active site (26, 30, 31). We now propose that the distorted active site of apo-IXa and the need for substrates to force it into an open conformation underlie the low activity of IXa.

A principal contribution of this study lies in the multiple structures of factor IXa revealing different functional states. The structure of the apo-form of IXa with free active site (PDB ID: 8EPH) provides the reference for structural comparisons to understand conformational effects caused by ligands. Comparing this reference state (ii) to the aptamer-bound structure with a free active site (i) and the structure where the active site is occupied by a substrate (iii) reveals the conformational ensemble arising from flexibility in the active site region (Fig. 2 A and C). In this ensemble, displacement of Trp215 and reorientation of the 215 to 225 polypeptide segment leads to a closure or opening of the S1 pocket, which can be allosterically modulated by exosite-binding ligands and by substrate.

The active site region of the apo-form of factor IXa (ii) was unexpectedly found in a latent conformation with an occluded S1 site. In combination with the features of the substrate-bound form (iii), it follows that the process of productive substrate binding to the enzyme must overcome the thermodynamic barrier associated with the movement of Trp215 and the 215 to 225 polypeptide backbone in order to engage the active site (Fig. 2C). Similarly, exosite-dependent allosteric inhibition by DTRI-177 likely exploits flexibility in the residues surrounding the active site and its already distorted conformation in apo-IXa to stabilize a further distorted and inhibited form of the protease. We are presently unable to distinguish whether the inhibition of factor IXa by DTRI-177 results from conformational trapping, induced-fit, or significant contributions from both mechanisms. Nevertheless, the observed kinetics of peptidyl substrate cleavage are consistent with the hypothesis that the closed active site can slowly relax into the open conformation in the presence of substrate.

Although ligand-dependent protease allostery has extensively been invoked to explain Na+ effects in thrombin or the effects of tissue factor on VIIa, crystal structures of native factors VIIa (PDB ID: 1KLJ), Xa (PDB ID: 1C5M), and thrombin (PDB ID: 3U69), all display an accessible S1 pocket ready to bind and process substrate (Fig. 2B). There is one reported structure of apo-thrombin (1JOU) with a partly displaced Trp215 that has been a component of the interpretation to explain the impaired properties of “slow” and Na+-free thrombin. This association remains ambiguous as this thrombin structure does contain bound Na+ and the 215 to 225 polypeptide segment remains in the appropriate configuration for an accessible S1 pocket. In contrast, the types of differences seen with IXa related to movements of Trp215 and the 220 region are evident in structures of the zymogen, prethrombin 2, and several engineered forms of thrombin with destabilizing mutations (SI Appendix, Fig. S7). In these cases, impaired function arising from the destabilizing mutations may be explained by a conformational shift favoring the closed state of S1 pocket. In line with this conclusion, changes in the orientation of Trp215 in VIIa, predicted from molecular dynamics, have been proposed to explain the enhanced activity of mutants of this protease (32). Overall, our findings with apo-IXa and the structural features of the other homologous coagulation proteases likely explains the uniquely poor catalytic activity of IXa thus addressing a longstanding question in the field (30, 33).

Conformational plasticity observed in the active site of factor IXa has parallels in the changes associated with the transition of zymogen to protease. As discovered in the classic work of Bode and Huber, trypsinogen (PDB ID: 2TGT) is converted into trypsin (PDB ID: 5MNZ) upon proteolytic activation driven by the nascent N terminus that causes the opening of the S1 pocket (34). The same process was also inferred for factor VIIa (PDB ID: 1JBU), thrombin (13), and factor Xa (35). However, in contrast to trypsin, serine proteases of the coagulation system seem to utilize a multilayer mechanism of activation, where the N terminus insertion is not sufficient for developing full active site function. It is possible that, after proteolytic activation, the active site of factor IXa can further be modulated in an exosite-dependent manner. In support of this idea, the allosteric control of thrombin activity involves the structurally related exosite, where Kringle domains bind to maintain its intermediate called “meizothrombin” in a zymogen-like state (36). Another example is found in protein kinases, which maintain the low activity state by using exosite-binding regulatory domains and which transition into the high activity state upon domain dissociation via a dynamic rearrangement of the active site (37). Therefore, the dynamic mechanism linking exosite binding and active site reactivity can be ubiquitously utilized by multiple classes of enzymes playing a vital role in health and disease.

In addition to binding DTRI-177, the exosite in the catalytic domain of IXa represents another interaction site important for intrinsic Xase function (24). Presumably, factor VIIIa binds to this exosite in an analogous way as tissue factor binds to VIIa and Va binds to Xa (10, 12). While factor VIIIa may utilize a similar shape complementarity mechanism to specifically recognize factor IXa as shown here for DTRI-177, the functional consequences are clearly different. Factor VIIIa minimally effects peptidyl substrate cleavage by IXa yet greatly enhances factor X activation (38). In addition to the allosteric mechanism delineated here for the inhibition of peptidyl substrate cleavage, DTRI-177 has been shown to be a potent inhibitor of X activation by IXa (21). DTRI-177 binds both zymogen and activated protease with a similar affinity (SI Appendix, Table S2) while factor VIIIa selectively interacts with IXa. Taken together, it seems likely that factor VIIIa utilizes additional interaction interfaces with factor IXa and factor X to achieve selectivity for IXa over the zymogen and enhance X activation by the intrinsic Xase complex. We speculate that these additional binding interactions facilitate presentation of the scissile bond in factor X to the active site of IXa regardless of whether factor VIIIa has additional allosteric effects, yet to be delineated, on the active site of IXa (38). Targeting the exosite in factor IXa with synthetic ligands may produce a potent anticoagulant effect (Fig. 3G). Such effects may result from interference with the productive interaction of IXa with VIIIa, as shown previously for heparin (39), and/or from allosteric inhibition of the protease active site, as we show here for DTRI-177.

The structural information complemented by functional studies has provided insights into steric and allosteric mechanisms at play in the regulation of a key protease of coagulation. This study further bears on the development of molecular probes by uncovering the determinants of specific target recognition by RNA aptamers on related exosite surfaces of coagulation proteases. Our finding of the exosite-mediated allosteric control of factor IXa, together with data on exosite mutations causing bleeding or prothrombotic phenotypes, demonstrate the importance of this functional site in the regulation of hemostasis and suggest unique ways to modulate hemostatic balance.

sec.title: Materials and Methods
sec.p: Recombinant variants of human factor IXa were expressed in mammalian cell culture, purified to homogeneity, and cocrystallized with DTRI-177 aptamer containing 2′-fluoro and 2′-OMe modifications. Structures were solved from X-ray diffraction data by molecular replacement. Prolongation of clotting was measured in commercial samples of human and animal plasma. The active site function of wild-type factor IXa was assessed by cleavage of fluorogenic substrate and reaction with antithrombin. Binding affinity of exosite ligands and variants of factor IXa was studied by biolayer interferometry, heparin-affinity chromatography, and fluorescence anisotropy. Detailed Materials and Methods can be found in SI Appendix.

caption.p: Atomic details of factor IXa – DTRI-177 interaction shown for the structure (PDB ID: 8EPK).

The movie is a morph between two structures: the apo-state of factor IXa with a latent, immature S1 binding pocket (PDB ID: 8EPH), and antithrombin-bound structure with the reactive center loop P1 Arg of antithrombin (green sticks) inserted into the open S1 pocket (PDB ID: 3KCG). The movie proceeds to show structural transitions undergone by the active site in order to accommodate the substrate. The movie starts by rendering factor IXa in the apo-state, with the overlaid reactive center loop of antithrombin, demonstrating that the substrate-like inhibitor cannot dock into the active site at the apo-state. To open the S1 pocket and accommodate the substrate analog, Trp215 of IXa (yellow) first moves out of the way.

The movie is a morph between two structures: the apo-state of factor IXa with a latent, immature S1 binding pocket (PDB ID: 8EPH), and DTRI-177 -bound structure (PDB ID: 8EPK). The movie proceeds to show structural transitions undergone by the active site upon the exosite binding by the RNA aptamer (top left corner; cyan). The movie starts by rendering factor IXa in the apo-state, with the overlaid structure of DTRI-177. The movie demonstrates that the exosite-binding aptamer causes a distortion in the active site, where Trp215 of IXa (yellow) flips to interact with catalytic His57 (purple) and completely closes the S1 pocket.
